epics.title: Mind Registration Service (Layer 2)
epics.description:
Spawned from the Nervous System migration (Phase A, 2026-05-14). Phase A removed MindRegistry.scan() — comms now reads minds only from broker.minds, and the routing table is populated by a single admin-bearer endpoint, POST /broker/minds, which is Layer 1. This epic is the user-facing layer on top: provisioning a mind end to end, not just writing a routing row.

The goal is a web UI hosted on the nervous-system machine that walks a user through bringing a new mind online. The endpoint behind it can also be called programmatically by another mind, so the same provisioning flow serves the first-time setup wizard and inter-mind orchestration.

Out of scope: Layer 1 routing registration, which already exists as POST /broker/minds and shipped in Phase A2; and removing or deprecating the bootstrap manual flow (the /hivemind:setup-* skills), which can coexist with the web UI until the UI is proven.
epics.requirements:
POST /minds/provision does the full setup, one endpoint internally layered: clone the appropriate template repo (hive_mind for containerised minds, the bare-metal template, or the remote template for off-host); scaffold minds/<name>/MIND.md with name, model, harness, gateway_url and install_path; generate the UUID, which is the mind's permanent mind_id; seed the soul into the lucent KG as one Mind node with soul_values plus per-class data class seed memories; install hooks on the target host, which is only possible when the target is the NS host, or via a remote installer the user runs on the target host after provisioning hands back a tarball; and internally call Layer 1 to write the routing row.

Cross-machine: the NS web UI is reachable from any remote machine that can reach the NS host, so remote installs work as long as the remote can hit the provision endpoint. The endpoint seeds the KG centrally and either installs hooks remotely via the remote-admin bridge or returns a tarball plus run instructions for the user to install locally on the target.
epics.acceptance_criteria: A mind provisions end to end from the UI or from another mind's call, and the same flow serves both. Resume by picking the auth-window model first; the rest cascades from that decision.
epics.qa_tests: The idempotency and auth-window decisions have to be settled before implementation, because both change the endpoint's contract. The cross-instance dispatch half is testable only with two NS installations, so the bearer-gating and the gateway_url reachability are the two properties to verify there.

features.title: The provisioning endpoint
features.description: POST /minds/provision, one endpoint internally layered over six steps.
features.requirements: Template clone, MIND.md scaffold, UUID generation, soul seeded into the KG, hooks installed on the target, and Layer 1 called to write the routing row. Three templates on day one: bare-metal (Skippy-shaped), containerised in the NS host's docker-compose (Ada-shaped), and remote (a new template) — the wizard asks which.
features.acceptance_criteria: A provisioned mind registers, dispatches a turn, and can be cleanly removed.
features.qa_tests: A provision produces a UUID, a broker row keyed to it, a KG Mind node keyed to the same UUID, a MIND.md and installed hooks. A mind with no KG Mind node answers as whoever the graph thinks owns the memories — the Hex-answering-as-Ada failure — so that node's existence is the test that matters most.

stories.title: Implement the six provisioning steps behind one endpoint
stories.description: Clone, scaffold, UUID, soul seed, hooks, routing row.
stories.requirements: All six, with a partial provision recoverable rather than left half-registered.
stories.acceptance_criteria: One call produces a working mind.
stories.qa_tests: Every artifact exists and is keyed to the same UUID. A failure midway leaves nothing partially registered.

stories.title: Support all three templates on day one
stories.description: Bare-metal, containerised, and remote. The wizard asks which.
stories.requirements: All three, since the remote one is new.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Each template produces a working mind of its kind.
stories.qa_tests: A provision of each shape produces a mind that registers and answers. The remote shape is the one with no prior art, so it needs the hooks-tarball path tested rather than assumed.

stories.title: Decide repo-clone scope: host-mounted directory or staged tarball
stories.description: The provision endpoint runs as the comms container user. Does it write into a host-mounted directory the user picked at install time, or stage a tarball the user unpacks at the destination of their choice? This affects whether comms needs broad host-write permission or stays sandboxed.
stories.requirements: A decision, weighing the permission the first option needs.
stories.acceptance_criteria: comms' host-write permission is a deliberate choice rather than a side effect.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. The artifact is the decision. Giving comms broad host write is the thing to decide knowingly.

stories.title: Decide the UI shape: Jinja-rendered HTML or a TypeScript SPA
stories.description: A FastAPI route returning Jinja-rendered HTML is enough for the bootstrap form; a real SPA only earns its complexity if we expect to manage many minds from the UI. Default to plain HTML.
stories.requirements: A decision.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The simpler option unless there is a reason.
stories.qa_tests: Not code.

features.title: Cross-instance message dispatch
features.description: Two NS installations — a workstation and NetSage, say — need to send messages to each other's minds, so Ada on Machine A can ask a mind on Machine B for a response the same way she asks a local mind today. The new NS centralises everything the old per-mind broker and gateway pair used to split: one comms service per NS holds the broker, the session manager and the HTTP dispatch. So cross-instance dispatch reduces to one NS's comms calling another NS's comms over the network — no federation protocol, just authenticated HTTP between peers.
features.requirements:
Three things have to be true in comms/sessions.py::_spawn, where the call is an HTTP post to the mind's URL. First, the target NS's comms endpoints — /sessions, /sessions/{id}/message, /messages — accept bearer-authenticated requests from peer NS instances. Second, the dispatching NS holds the peer's API key in its keyring, scoped to the registered mind, and _spawn injects it on the request. Third, the mind's gateway_url resolves to an address the peer can actually reach: host network, not docker network.

Auth on the receiving side: comms' /sessions and /messages, and the spawn endpoints on individual mind containers, currently accept unauthenticated requests because they only see docker-internal traffic. Once any mind is reachable from off-host, those endpoints need bearer-gating using the existing admin bearer model, the same pattern as the lucent admin endpoints, with local intra-NS calls continuing to work as long as they include the bearer. Note that the session-token work has since closed this for the mind side — every mind now 401s an unauthenticated /sessions call — so what remains here is the comms-to-comms peer leg.

Error handling: the existing contract applies, so an unreachable peer returns 503 mind_unreachable and the caller decides whether to retry. Transient cross-network failures are more common than local ones, so consider a small bounded retry of two or three attempts with backoff inside _spawn for remote dispatches only, with local calls staying fast-fail.
features.acceptance_criteria: A mind on one NS can message a mind on another, authenticated, with an unreachable peer reported as 503 rather than folded into something else.
features.qa_tests: A cross-instance dispatch succeeds with the peer bearer and is refused without it. An unreachable peer returns 503 mind_unreachable rather than a shape meaning the mind is down or has nothing to say — folding a refusal into a different shape is how a remedy gets applied to the wrong machine.

stories.title: Bearer-gate comms' session and message endpoints for peer instances
stories.description: They currently accept unauthenticated requests because they only see docker-internal traffic. The same pattern as the lucent admin endpoints.
stories.requirements: Local intra-NS calls keep working as long as they include the bearer.
stories.acceptance_criteria: An off-host caller without a bearer is refused.
stories.qa_tests: An unauthenticated peer call is refused. An authenticated one succeeds. Local calls carrying the bearer are unaffected.

stories.title: Store and inject the peer bearer per registered mind
stories.description: Scoped in the keyring to the registered mind, read by _spawn at send time.
stories.requirements: Per-mind scoping, so one peer's credential does not open another.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A dispatch to a remote mind carries that mind's peer credential.
stories.qa_tests: A dispatch injects the right credential. A mind with no stored peer credential fails loudly rather than sending unauthenticated.

stories.title: Add a bounded retry for remote dispatches only
stories.description: Two or three attempts with backoff, since transient cross-network failures are more common than local ones. Local calls stay fast-fail.
stories.requirements: Remote only.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A transient network blip does not surface as an unreachable mind.
stories.qa_tests: A remote dispatch that fails once then succeeds completes. A local dispatch failure is immediate. A genuinely unreachable peer still reports 503 after the attempts rather than retrying forever.

features.title: The reachability decision
features.description: An open design question /minds/provision has to settle. Option A defaults every mind to a host-reachable address, so gateway_url is always the host's LAN or WAN address — simpler, no per-mind branching, no extra wizard step, and every mind callable from off-host by default, with the trade-off that the mind's port is bound to the host interface even when no peer will ever call it. Option B asks explicitly at provision time whether the mind is reachable from outside this host: if no, a docker-network address, which is current behaviour and means the mind is only callable from inside the local docker network; if yes, a host-network address. The trade-off is an extra question, and if the user says no for one mind and later adds a mind on another machine, the second cannot reach the first until the first is re-registered.
features.requirements: Pick one and bake it into the wizard. The default leaning is B, with a hint saying to say yes unless you have a reason not to — it exposes one more port per mind only on consent, and the failure mode, no answer until re-register, is obvious.
features.acceptance_criteria: One option chosen and implemented, with the failure mode visible rather than silent.
features.qa_tests: Under B, a mind registered as not externally reachable is genuinely unreachable from a peer, and the error says so rather than timing out opaquely.

stories.title: Pick Option A or B and bake it into the wizard
stories.description: Default leaning B, with a hint to say yes unless there is a reason not to.
stories.requirements: A decision, with the failure mode made obvious in the UI.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A user cannot accidentally make a mind unreachable without being told what that means.
stories.qa_tests: Under B, the wizard's hint is present and the no-path's consequence is stated. A peer call to an unreachable mind reports why.

features.title: Provisioning additions for cross-instance
features.description: Two responsibilities /minds/provision grows once cross-instance dispatch exists.
features.requirements: Capture peer credentials: when the user registers a mind that lives on a different NS instance — the remote template, or any case where the target host is not this one — the wizard prompts for that peer's admin bearer and stores it in the keyring scoped to the mind, with the local comms dispatcher reading it at send time. And a bidirectional registration nudge: when the wizard registers a remote mind into this NS, surface a prompt saying that for that mind to reach minds on this host, they also need registering on the peer, and offer to generate the reverse-direction MIND.md stubs for the user to copy across. That second one is an optional convenience.
features.acceptance_criteria: Registering a remote mind captures what the dispatcher will need, and the user is told that registration is one-directional.
features.qa_tests: A remote registration prompts for the peer bearer and stores it scoped to the mind. The nudge appears, since the one-directional nature of registration is exactly the thing a user discovers weeks later otherwise.

stories.title: Prompt for and store the peer admin bearer on a remote registration
stories.description: Scoped in the keyring to the mind, read by the dispatcher at send time.
stories.requirements: Prompted at provision time, not discovered at first dispatch.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The dispatcher has what it needs before the first send.
stories.qa_tests: A remote registration without a captured bearer cannot dispatch, and the wizard does not let it reach that state silently.

stories.title: Offer the reverse-direction MIND.md stubs
stories.description: An optional convenience: generate the reverse-direction set so the user can copy them onto the peer host.
stories.requirements: Optional, and clearly labelled as something to run on the other machine.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The user knows registration is one-directional.
stories.qa_tests: The prompt appears on a remote registration and the generated stubs are valid on the peer.

features.title: Loose ends to firm up before implementation
features.description: Three decisions, one of which gates the rest.
features.requirements: Setup-mode auth window: on first-mind bootstrap there is no admin bearer yet, so there needs to be a setup mode that opens an unauthed window once, generates COMMS_ADMIN_BEARER_TOKEN after the first mind is provisioned, and closes the window. Should it be a manual flag, a time-boxed window after a fresh container start, or a one-time passphrase shown by the installer? There is a security risk if left open. And idempotency on name collision: if a name or UUID already exists, return 409 with the existing UUID, or overwrite? Default 409 — minds are durable and accidental overwrites destroy soul continuity.
features.acceptance_criteria: The auth-window model is picked first, because the rest cascades from that decision.
features.qa_tests: The window closes after the first provision and cannot be reopened without the chosen mechanism. A duplicate name returns 409 naming the existing UUID rather than overwriting a mind's soul.

stories.title: Pick the setup-mode auth window model
stories.description: A manual flag, a time-boxed window after a fresh container start, or a one-time passphrase shown by the installer. There is a security risk if left open, and this decision gates the rest of the epic.
stories.requirements: A model that cannot be left open by accident.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The window closes on its own or on the first provision, never by someone remembering.
stories.qa_tests: After the first mind is provisioned, an unauthenticated provision is refused. A window left unused also closes.

stories.title: Return 409 on a name or UUID collision
stories.description: Default 409 with the existing UUID, not overwrite. Minds are durable and accidental overwrites destroy soul continuity.
stories.requirements: 409 naming the existing UUID.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No provision can overwrite an existing mind.
stories.qa_tests: A duplicate name returns 409 carrying the existing UUID. The mind's soul is untouched.

epics.title: The TUI Mind
epics.description:
Why: at the time this was written, every surface — Telegram and the web 'terminal' — talked to a mind through hive-comms, which spawned the mind's harness headless in stream-JSON mode, parsed the JSON and relayed plain text. The web terminal was not attached to any CLI; it was a chat relay dressed as a terminal. The want was a real rich terminal: the harness's actual interactive interface, with boxes, slash menus, streaming and key handling, reachable both directly on the host and emulated over the web, for every mind.

Much of Parts 1 and 2 has since shipped by a different route. The tmux-backed browser terminal exists — WS /sessions/{id}/attach-pty bridging raw bytes between an xterm.js tile and an interactive harness CLI, with the conversation living in tmux and a tile as a client, setsid plus TIOCSCTTY so SIGWINCH reaches the app, exact-match tmux targets, a NUL heartbeat, and in-place pane rotation. What remains genuinely open from this document is Part 3: moving prompt composition out of hive-comms and into each mind's hooks.

This document scoped a brand-new containerized mind as the test bed — prove the pattern on one disposable mind, then generalize to the rest of the hive. A standard containerized mind, operator-class access not required, since it is a sequestered test subject rather than a twin, running one harness inside its container with its own .claude or .codex directory holding its skills, hooks and identity. The only unusual thing about it is that it exposes its harness's interactive terminal rather than just the headless stream.
epics.requirements:
Part 1, TUI directly on the host: let an operator at the host attach to a live interactive harness session inside the container, with a real pseudo-terminal so the CLI renders its full TUI. Launch the harness interactively under a PTY inside the container with docker exec -it, run in the mind's working directory with the mind's environment — MIND_ID, MIND_NAME, the same hook config the headless path uses — where -it gives it the TTY it needs to draw the TUI. That session is a separate session from the ones hive-comms drives and does not go through the gateway; it is the operator sitting in the cockpit of that mind's harness directly. Per-turn memory hooks — capture, contextual retrieval, standing rules, rotation — still fire because they live in the mind's harness config and fire on any session in that environment, but bootstrap composition does not, which is what Part 3 is about. The deliverable is a documented one-liner or thin wrapper script per mind, with no new service for the host path since it is just an attach.

Part 2, web TUI emulation: the same interactive session reachable from a browser, which is the ttyd pattern. A PTY bridge over a websocket — a small process that on connect execs the harness interactively inside the target mind's container under a PTY, then pipes the PTY's bytes to the websocket and the websocket's bytes back, forwarding key events and terminal resize events too. The browser runs xterm.js, which already speaks ANSI escapes, cursor addressing and the alternate screen buffer, so the harness's TUI renders faithfully; the page lets you pick which mind to attach to, each mind having its own websocket endpoint that execs into that mind's container. The candidate placement is a single small service on the hive's Docker network that can docker exec into any mind container, with auth and exposure scoped to the host or LAN since this is an operator tool rather than a public surface. It supersedes the chat-relay web terminal for operator use while the relay stays for normal conversation, where you want comms doing the assembly.

Part 3, move prompt composition from hive-comms into each mind's hooks: the interactive paths bypass hive-comms and so lose the bootstrap composition comms does today, which is the point rather than a regret. Composition should leave hive-comms entirely and become each mind's own responsibility, so comms collapses to a pure router and broker.
epics.acceptance_criteria:
The end state: with the three blocks in a SessionStart hook and standing and contextual already in the UserPromptSubmit hook, every path — interactive TUI, web TUI and the existing headless relay — gets identical context, because context now comes from the mind's hooks regardless of who spawned the session. hive-comms keeps session management, brokering, HITL and remote control, and loses prompt composition entirely: compose_prompt_blocks, system_prompt_blocks on the dispatch payload, and the bootstrap_loader composition path all get deleted in the same pass that moves them.

Sequence: stand up the test mind; Part 1's host attach wrapper; Part 3 on that one mind, building the SessionStart composition hook and relocating the rotation carry-forward storage so the interactive session boots with full context, verified against a comms-driven session for parity; Part 2's bridge and page; then generalize by rolling the hook to every mind and deleting composition from hive-comms.
epics.qa_tests: Parity against a comms-driven session is the gate for Part 3 — the hook-composed context and the comms-composed context have to match before composition can be deleted from comms. Note that the hook must emit hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext rather than systemMessage, because systemMessage is UI-only and silently never reaches the model.

features.title: Part 1 — TUI directly on the host
features.description: An operator attaching to a live interactive harness session inside the container, under a real pseudo-terminal. Largely overtaken by the tmux-backed terminal, which starts the CLI inside tmux on a dedicated socket, but the bare host-attach wrapper is still the simplest path for an operator at the machine.
features.requirements: docker exec -it into the container, in the mind's working directory with the mind's environment and the same hook config the headless path uses. A separate session from the ones comms drives, not going through the gateway.
features.acceptance_criteria: The TUI renders fully, and per-turn hooks still fire because they live in the mind's harness config.
features.qa_tests: The harness draws its boxes and slash menus. A turn in the attached session fires the capture and contextual-retrieval hooks. Bootstrap composition does not, which is the gap Part 3 closes rather than a bug.

stories.title: Write a per-mind host attach wrapper
stories.description: A documented one-liner or thin script that docker exec -it's into the mind and launches the harness with the right environment and cwd. No new service.
stories.requirements: Right cwd, right environment, a real TTY.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The TUI renders.
stories.qa_tests: Judged by attaching and looking at it. Per-turn hooks fire; bootstrap composition does not.

features.title: Part 2 — web TUI emulation
features.description: Shipped by a different route. The tmux-backed browser terminal now does this: WS /sessions/{id}/attach-pty bridges raw bytes between an xterm.js tile and the harness CLI, the conversation lives in tmux so ending a client detaches the view without touching the conversation, tmux owns the screen model and history, setsid plus TIOCSCTTY makes SIGWINCH actually reach the app, tmux targets use the exact-match form, and a NUL heartbeat every 5 seconds makes half-open mobile connections detectable. What this document proposed — one bridge service that docker execs into any mind container — is not the shape that landed; each mind exposes its own attach route instead, which is why a container, a bare-metal mind and a mind across the LAN are one code path.
features.requirements: Retained for the record. The remaining question from this part is whether the chat-relay surface and the pty surface coexist as the doc intended — relay for everyday talk, web TUI for hands-on driving — which they do, with cross-surface pickup moving a conversation between them.
features.acceptance_criteria: Already met by the shipped terminal.
features.qa_tests: Covered by the terminal's own work. The design difference worth keeping in mind: a per-mind attach route rather than one bridge with docker exec, which is what makes a mind on another machine work at all.

stories.title: Web TUI over a PTY bridge
stories.description: Shipped as the tmux-backed browser terminal, by a different design than this document proposed — a per-mind attach route rather than one central bridge that docker execs into containers. The per-mind shape is why a bare-metal mind and a mind across the LAN work on the same code path.
stories.requirements: xterm.js in the browser, raw bytes over a websocket, resize forwarded.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A tile attaches and the TUI paints.
stories.qa_tests: Covered by the terminal's own tests and live use.

features.title: Part 3 — move prompt composition into each mind's hooks
features.description: The genuinely open part. comms/bootstrap_loader's compose_prompt_blocks builds three blocks and ships them to the mind's mind_server as system_prompt_blocks, which become the harness's appended system prompt: <soul>, the Mind node's soul_values array read from the lucent KG by the mind's UUID; <recent-memory>, the top-20 decay-weighted contextual rows from lucent's /memory/recent-decayed for this mind, the initial prime; and <session-memory>, the latest rotation carry-forward for this mind and client_ref, read from comms' own session_memory SQLite table, including the late-turn-handoff continuation list of user turns accepted after rotation began, rendered as a pending-input block. Standing rules are already out of comms — they ride in per turn via the contextual_retrieval UserPromptSubmit hook, which also does contextual similarity retrieval — so Part 3 only has to relocate those three blocks.
features.requirements: A per-mind SessionStart hook for first-turn bootstrap that reproduces the three blocks and emits them as hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, not systemMessage, which never reaches the model. soul: fetch the Mind node's soul_values from the KG by MIND_ID and render the block — a pure lucent read, a direct port of _fetch_soul. recent-memory: call lucent's /memory/recent-decayed with the mind id and a limit of 20 and render the block — a direct port of _fetch_recent_memory. session-memory: the carry-forward currently lives in comms' SQLite, written by the rotation_check Stop hook, so for a hook to read it without comms in the loop the storage has to move somewhere the mind can reach directly — either a lucent endpoint or a per-mind store — with rotation_check repointed to write there. That is the one piece that is not a pure read-port; it needs a small storage relocation, and that endpoint is specified as part of this work.
features.acceptance_criteria: Every path gets identical context. compose_prompt_blocks, system_prompt_blocks on the dispatch payload, and the bootstrap_loader composition path are deleted in the same pass that moves them.
features.qa_tests: Parity against a comms-driven session is the gate: the hook-composed context and the comms-composed context match before anything is deleted from comms. The systemMessage trap is the one to avoid — a hook emitting it looks correct in the UI and silently never reaches the model.

stories.title: Port the soul block into a SessionStart hook
stories.description: Fetch the Mind node's soul_values from the KG by MIND_ID and render <soul>. A pure lucent read, a direct port of _fetch_soul.
stories.requirements: Emitted as hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, never systemMessage.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The soul reaches the model on an interactive session.
stories.qa_tests: The hook's output matches comms' composed block. A systemMessage emission would pass a UI check and fail this one, which is why the comparison is against what the model received.

stories.title: Port the recent-memory block into the same hook
stories.description: Call /memory/recent-decayed with the mind id and limit 20, render <recent-memory>. A direct port of _fetch_recent_memory.
stories.requirements: Same decay weighting, same limit.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The initial prime matches what comms composed.
stories.qa_tests: The two blocks are comparable for the same mind at the same moment.

stories.title: Relocate the rotation carry-forward so a hook can read it
stories.description: The carry-forward lives in comms' SQLite today, written by the rotation_check Stop hook. For a hook to read it without comms in the loop, the storage has to move to a lucent endpoint or a per-mind store, with rotation_check repointed to write there. The one piece that is not a pure read-port.
stories.requirements: Specify the endpoint as part of this work. The continuation list — user turns accepted after rotation began, rendered as a pending-input block — has to travel with it.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A hook can compose <session-memory> with comms out of the loop.
stories.qa_tests: A rotation writes to the new store and the hook reads it back, continuation list included. The carry-forward is soul, recent memory and the last exchange in one string, so whatever holds it must be guarded accordingly rather than exposed on a bulk listing.

stories.title: Verify parity against a comms-driven session
stories.description: Before anything is deleted. Step 3 of the sequence, on the one test mind.
stories.requirements: The interactive session boots with full context matching the comms-driven path.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No block differs.
stories.qa_tests: Compare what the model received on both paths for the same mind and the same conversation. A difference is a finding rather than an acceptable variance, because the deletion that follows is irreversible.

stories.title: Roll the hook to every mind, then delete composition from comms
stories.description: Step 5. compose_prompt_blocks, system_prompt_blocks on the dispatch payload, and the bootstrap_loader composition path all go in the same pass.
stories.requirements: Every mind on the hook before the deletion.
stories.acceptance_criteria: comms keeps session management, brokering, HITL and remote control, and loses prompt composition entirely.
stories.qa_tests: Every mind's interactive and headless paths compose identically. A grep finds no caller of the deleted composition path. One mind left behind would lose its context silently, so the rollout is verified per mind before the delete.

stories.title: Answer the four open questions
stories.description: Bridge service language and runtime, which Part 2's actual implementation has since settled. Where the relocated carry-forward lives — a lucent endpoint versus per-mind. The auth model for the web TUI endpoint — LAN-only, token, or both, which the session-token work has since answered for the shipped terminal. And whether the headless relay path also switches to hook-composed context at cutover, or keeps system_prompt_blocks until the very end as a fallback.
stories.requirements: The two still open are the carry-forward's home and the relay's cutover timing.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Both decided before the relocation is built.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. The artifacts are the decisions.
